properties.title: Kingdom of Nueva Galicia c. 1550
properties.label: Nueva Galicia
properties.description: The territory Nuño de Guzmán overran in 1530–31 was named the Kingdom of Nueva Galicia in 1531 and given its own audiencia in 1548, first at Compostela and from 1560 at Guadalajara. It ran from the Pacific coast of Nayarit inland to the silver mines of Zacatecas, and its northern edge was an open frontier with the unconquered peoples of the Gran Chichimeca. Nueva Galicia stayed a separate kingdom within New Spain throughout the colonial period.
properties.note: Drawn as the union of the modern states of Jalisco, Nayarit, Zacatecas and Aguascalientes, the usual short description of the kingdom's stable extent and a rough stand-in for Gerhard's map of Nueva Galicia (The North Frontier of New Spain). It overstates the kingdom in the south, where the provinces of Ávalos, Autlán, Amula and Tuxpan (around Sayula, Zapotlán and Autlán) and Colima's hinterland belonged to Nueva España. It understates it in the northwest, where the province of Culiacán (Sinaloa) also belonged to Nueva Galicia; Sinaloa is left out because most of it was unconquered in 1550. The northern limit was an undefined war frontier.

sources.citation: Peter Gerhard, The North Frontier of New Spain, rev. ed. (University of Oklahoma Press, 1993).
Ida Altman, The War for Mexico's West: Indians and Spaniards in New Galicia, 1524–1550 (University of New Mexico Press, 2010).

properties.title: The Gran Chichimeca during the Chichimeca War (1550–1590)
properties.label: Gran Chichimeca
properties.description: North of the Lerma River and the Bajío lay the dry plateau the Spaniards called the Gran Chichimeca, home to mobile hunter-gatherer and farming peoples (Guachichiles, Zacatecos, Guamares, Pames and others) who had never been part of the Mesoamerican states. When the silver road to Zacatecas cut through their lands, they raided its wagon trains and towns from 1550 for forty years. The Spaniards answered with forts and defensive towns along the road and enslaved captives as prisoners of "war by fire and blood", until the Third Mexican Provincial Council (1585) questioned the war's justice; finally, from 1585–90, they turned to a policy of negotiated peace, gifts of food and clothing, missions and Tlaxcalan settlers.
properties.note: A rough outline of the war zone after the map in Powell (1952): from the Bajío north to about Saltillo and Mapimí, between the Sierra Madre Occidental and the Sierra Madre Oriental. The peoples of the region had no common territory, and the war zone moved north over time.

sources.citation: Philip Wayne Powell, Soldiers, Indians, and Silver: The Northward Advance of New Spain, 1550–1600 (University of California Press, 1952).
Peter Gerhard, The North Frontier of New Spain, rev. ed. (University of Oklahoma Press, 1993).
Paul Gillingham, Mexico: A 500-Year History (Atlantic Monthly Press, 2025), chs. 1, 2 and 7.

properties.title: Mexico City rebuilt on the ruins of Tenochtitlan
properties.label: Mexico City
properties.description: After the siege Cortés governed from Coyoacán, on the lakeshore, but chose to rebuild the capital on the ruined island, keeping the prestige and the defensible site of the Mexica city. A grid (traza) for Spanish residents, planned by Alonso García Bravo, was laid out around the old ceremonial centre, with the Indigenous wards (San Juan Tenochtitlan and Santiago Tlatelolco) around it, and the town council moved in from Coyoacán in 1524. The decision tied the colonial capital to the lake and, for three centuries, to the problem of flooding.
properties.note: Marked at the Zócalo, the plaza at the centre of the traza, laid out over the southern part of the Mexica ceremonial precinct.

sources.citation: Barbara E. Mundy, The Death of Aztec Tenochtitlan, the Life of Mexico City (University of Texas Press, 2015).
Charles Gibson, The Aztecs under Spanish Rule: A History of the Indians of the Valley of Mexico, 1519–1810 (Stanford University Press, 1964).
Michael C. Meyer, William L. Sherman and Susan M. Deeds, The Course of Mexican History, 10th ed. (Oxford University Press, 2014).
Paul Gillingham, Mexico: A 500-Year History (Atlantic Monthly Press, 2025), ch. 5.

properties.title: The Twelve Franciscans walk to Mexico City
properties.label: The Twelve Franciscans
properties.description: Twelve Franciscan friars led by Martín de Valencia landed at San Juan de Ulúa in May 1524 and walked barefoot up to Mexico City, where Cortés knelt to greet them in June. Their arrival opened the first, intensive phase of the "spiritual conquest": the friars spread out from the Valley of Mexico and the Puebla–Tlaxcala valley, baptised on a vast scale and learned Indigenous languages. Dominicans followed in 1526 and Augustinians in 1533.
properties.note: Only the landing (13 or 14 May 1524) and the arrival in Mexico City (17 or 18 June) are documented; the friars are usually said to have passed through Tlaxcala, which is the one intermediate vertex. The line across the mountains is schematic.

sources.citation: Robert Ricard, The Spiritual Conquest of Mexico: An Essay on the Apostolate and the Evangelizing Methods of the Mendicant Orders in New Spain, 1523–1572, trans. Lesley Byrd Simpson (University of California Press, 1966).
Paul Gillingham, Mexico: A 500-Year History (Atlantic Monthly Press, 2025), ch. 3.

properties.title: Pánuco: Santisteban del Puerto
properties.label: Pánuco
properties.description: Cortés himself led a campaign into the Huasteca on the lower Pánuco River in 1522 and founded the town of Santisteban del Puerto there, partly to forestall rival claims to the Gulf coast from Jamaica. Pánuco became a separate province under Nuño de Guzmán as governor (appointed 1525, arrived 1527), who exported enslaved Huastecs to the Caribbean before he turned west.
properties.note: Marked at the modern town of Pánuco, Veracruz; Gerhard places the Spanish villa on the river near here.

sources.citation: Peter Gerhard, A Guide to the Historical Geography of New Spain, rev. ed. (University of Oklahoma Press, 1993).
Hugh Thomas, Conquest: Montezuma, Cortés, and the Fall of Old Mexico (Simon & Schuster, 1993).

properties.title: Pedro de Alvarado's invasion of Guatemala
properties.label: Alvarado 1523–24
properties.description: Cortés sent Pedro de Alvarado south with a few hundred Spaniards and several thousand Nahua and other allies. They went by the Isthmus of Tehuantepec and Soconusco onto the Pacific slope, defeated the K'iche' in battles near Xelajú (Quetzaltenango) in February 1524, burned the K'iche' capital Q'umarkaj (Utatlán) and its rulers, and were received by their Kaqchikel allies at Iximché in April. Alvarado declared Iximché a Spanish town in July, but Spanish demands soon turned the Kaqchikel against him.
properties.note: Main stops only. The route through Oaxaca to Tehuantepec is assumed; the Guatemalan stops follow Alvarado's letters and the Nahua and Maya accounts in Restall & Asselbergs. Sources differ on battle dates.

sources.citation: Matthew Restall and Florine Asselbergs, Invading Guatemala: Spanish, Nahua, and Maya Accounts of the Conquest Wars (Pennsylvania State University Press, 2007).
Hugh Thomas, Conquest: Montezuma, Cortés, and the Fall of Old Mexico (Simon & Schuster, 1993).
Paul Gillingham, Mexico: A 500-Year History (Atlantic Monthly Press, 2025), chs. 1 and 2.

properties.title: Santiago founded at Iximché
properties.label: Iximché
properties.description: At the Kaqchikel capital Alvarado founded the first Spanish town in Guatemala, Santiago de los Caballeros. The Kaqchikel abandoned the city in August 1524 and fought the Spaniards for several years; the capital moved to Almolonga in 1527 and, after a mudslide destroyed it in 1541, to the valley of Panchoy (Antigua). Guatemala became a separate audiencia, and Chiapas and Soconusco were governed from it until 1821.
properties.note: Marked at the archaeological site of Iximché, about 3 km south of the modern town of Tecpán. Sources give 25 or 27 July 1524 for the founding of the town; only the month is shown.

sources.citation: Matthew Restall and Florine Asselbergs, Invading Guatemala: Spanish, Nahua, and Maya Accounts of the Conquest Wars (Pennsylvania State University Press, 2007).

properties.title: Cortés's march to Honduras (the Hibueras expedition)
properties.label: Cortés to Honduras
properties.description: In 1524 Cortés sent Cristóbal de Olid by sea to Honduras (Las Hibueras), and Olid declared himself independent. Cortés set out overland in October 1524 with Cuauhtémoc and other Mexica lords as hostages, by way of Coatzacoalcos, the swamps and rivers of Tabasco, the Chontal Maya kingdom of Acalan and the Itzá capital on Lake Petén, reaching the Gulf of Honduras in 1525 to find Olid already killed by his own men. The march showed how impassable the southern lowlands were, and Cortés's long absence let his enemies take over the government in Mexico; he returned by sea in 1526.
properties.note: Main stops only, after Cortés's Fifth Letter: Orizaba, Espíritu Santo (Coatzacoalcos), Tabasco (schematic), Itzamkanac in Acalan, Nojpetén (Flores) on Lake Petén Itzá, Nito near the mouth of the Río Dulce (marked at Livingston) and Trujillo. The return voyage via Havana to Veracruz is not drawn. Gillingham (ch. 2) gives the force as some 400 Spaniards and 3,000 Mexica and has Cortés convalesce for three months in Guatemala before going home; Cortés's Fifth Letter and Thomas have him sail from Trujillo via Havana to the Veracruz coast in 1526.

sources.citation: Hernán Cortés, Fifth Letter to Charles V (3 Sept 1526), in Letters from Mexico, trans. and ed. Anthony Pagden (Yale University Press, 1986).
Hugh Thomas, Conquest: Montezuma, Cortés, and the Fall of Old Mexico (Simon & Schuster, 1993).
Peter Gerhard, The Southeast Frontier of New Spain, rev. ed. (University of Oklahoma Press, 1993).
Paul Gillingham, Mexico: A 500-Year History (Atlantic Monthly Press, 2025), chs. 1, 2 and 5.

properties.title: Execution of Cuauhtémoc in Acalan
properties.label: Cuauhtémoc executed
properties.description: During the march to Honduras Cortés, told of a plot by the captive Mexica lords to rise against the Spaniards, had Cuauhtémoc, the last tlatoani of Tenochtitlan, and the lord of Tlacopan hanged in the Chontal Maya province of Acalan. Whether a plot existed is doubted by many historians.
properties.note: Marked at the El Tigre archaeological site on the Candelaria River, usually identified with Itzamkanac, the capital of Acalan. Some sources place the execution at another Acalan town (Taxahá). The date is traditionally 28 February 1525.

sources.citation: Hernán Cortés, Fifth Letter to Charles V (3 Sept 1526), in Letters from Mexico, trans. and ed. Anthony Pagden (Yale University Press, 1986).
Hugh Thomas, Conquest: Montezuma, Cortés, and the Fall of Old Mexico (Simon & Schuster, 1993).
Paul Gillingham, Mexico: A 500-Year History (Atlantic Monthly Press, 2025), ch. 1.

properties.title: Veracruz moves to La Antigua
properties.label: La Antigua
properties.description: The Villa Rica de la Vera Cruz, first founded on the beach in 1519 and then at Quiahuiztlan, was moved to the bank of the Huitzilapan (Antigua) River a few kilometres from the sea, where it stayed for most of the century. Ships anchored off the island of San Juan de Ulúa and goods were carried to the town by boat and along the coast. The road from here to the capital via Xalapa and Puebla was New Spain's main link with Spain.
properties.note: Sources date the move between 1523 and 1525.

sources.citation: Peter Gerhard, A Guide to the Historical Geography of New Spain, rev. ed. (University of Oklahoma Press, 1993).

properties.title: Ciudad Real (San Cristóbal) founded in Chiapas
properties.label: Ciudad Real
properties.description: Diego de Mazariegos, sent from Mexico to subdue the highlands of Chiapas, founded a Spanish villa in the cool valley of Jovel in 1528, later named Ciudad Real. It became the seat of the bishopric of Chiapas, whose bishop Bartolomé de las Casas fought the colonists over Indigenous labour in 1545–46. Chiapas was governed from Guatemala rather than Mexico until independence.
properties.note: Founded on 31 March 1528 according to most sources; only the year is shown.
properties.modern_place: San Cristóbal de las Casas, Chiapas, Mexico

sources.citation: Peter Gerhard, The Southeast Frontier of New Spain, rev. ed. (University of Oklahoma Press, 1993).

properties.title: Montejo's first entrada: Salamanca de Xelhá
properties.label: Xelhá 1527
properties.description: Francisco de Montejo, who held a royal contract to conquer Yucatán, landed on the east coast in autumn 1527 and founded Salamanca de Xelhá, the first Spanish town on the peninsula. His march through the northeastern Maya provinces (Ekab, Conil, Chauaca) ended in a hard-fought battle at Aké in 1528, and with disease and desertion thinning his force he withdrew. Yucatán had no central state to capture, and each of its sixteen or so Maya provinces had to be fought or bargained with separately.
properties.note: Marked at Xel-Há; the exact site of the Spanish camp is not known. The battle of Aké is not mapped: Chamberlain's Aké lay near Tizimín and is not securely identified.

sources.citation: Robert S. Chamberlain, The Conquest and Colonization of Yucatan, 1517–1550 (Carnegie Institution of Washington, 1948).
Inga Clendinnen, Ambivalent Conquests: Maya and Spaniard in Yucatan, 1517–1570 (Cambridge University Press, 1987).
Peter Gerhard, The Southeast Frontier of New Spain, rev. ed. (University of Oklahoma Press, 1993).
Paul Gillingham, Mexico: A 500-Year History (Atlantic Monthly Press, 2025), ch. 2.

properties.title: Montejo the Younger at Chichén Itzá
properties.label: Ciudad Real (Chichén Itzá)
properties.description: In the second campaign, launched from Campeche on the west coast in 1531, Montejo's son Francisco de Montejo the Younger marched into the Cupul province and set up a Spanish town called Ciudad Real among the ruins of Chichén Itzá. The Cupul besieged it in mid-1533 and the Spaniards fled; by 1535 they had abandoned the peninsula entirely.

sources.citation: Robert S. Chamberlain, The Conquest and Colonization of Yucatan, 1517–1550 (Carnegie Institution of Washington, 1948).
Inga Clendinnen, Ambivalent Conquests: Maya and Spaniard in Yucatan, 1517–1570 (Cambridge University Press, 1987).

properties.title: Chetumal: Gonzalo Guerrero and the Maya resistance
properties.label: Chetumal (Gonzalo Guerrero)
properties.description: Gonzalo Guerrero, a sailor shipwrecked off Yucatán in 1511, became a war captain of the Maya lord of Chetumal, married into his family and refused to rejoin the Spaniards when Cortés and then Montejo invited him. Chetumal, on the bay at the southern end of the peninsula, saw off Montejo's approach by sea in 1528 and made the Spanish town of Villa Real, which Alonso Dávila set up there in 1531, untenable within two years. Guerrero died about 1536 in Honduras, fighting the Spaniards alongside the people of the Ulúa valley. Gillingham opens his book with Guerrero and his fellow castaway Jerónimo de Aguilar, the interpreter who joined Cortés at Cozumel.
properties.note: Marked at modern Chetumal. The site of the Maya capital of Chactemal is debated: Santa Rita Corozal in Belize, about 14 km to the south, is often proposed, and Oxtankah, north of the modern city, is another candidate. Most accounts date Guerrero's death to 1536; Gillingham (Introduction) gives 1534 or 1535.

sources.citation: Robert S. Chamberlain, The Conquest and Colonization of Yucatan, 1517–1550 (Carnegie Institution of Washington, 1948).
Inga Clendinnen, Ambivalent Conquests: Maya and Spaniard in Yucatan, 1517–1570 (Cambridge University Press, 1987).
Peter Gerhard, The Southeast Frontier of New Spain, rev. ed. (University of Oklahoma Press, 1993).
Paul Gillingham, Mexico: A 500-Year History (Atlantic Monthly Press, 2025), Introduction.

properties.title: San Francisco de Campeche founded
properties.label: Campeche
properties.description: Montejo the Younger began the third, successful campaign from Campeche, on the Gulf coast at the Maya town of Ah Kin Pech, where he set up the first permanent Spanish town council in Yucatán. Campeche became the peninsula's port, exporting cotton cloth, wax and logwood.
properties.note: Local tradition gives 4 October 1540 for the founding; Chamberlain dates the town council to early 1541.
properties.modern_place: San Francisco de Campeche, Campeche, Mexico

sources.citation: Robert S. Chamberlain, The Conquest and Colonization of Yucatan, 1517–1550 (Carnegie Institution of Washington, 1948).
Peter Gerhard, The Southeast Frontier of New Spain, rev. ed. (University of Oklahoma Press, 1993).

properties.title: Mérida founded at T'Hó
properties.label: Mérida
properties.description: Montejo the Younger founded Mérida on the site of the Maya city of T'Hó (Ichcaansihó), reusing the stone of its platforms; the cathedral and Franciscan convent were built from them. The Xiu lords of Maní allied with the Spaniards, and a Maya coalition was defeated at T'Hó in 1542. Mérida became the capital of the province of Yucatán, which was governed largely apart from Mexico because of the difficulty of overland travel.

sources.citation: Robert S. Chamberlain, The Conquest and Colonization of Yucatan, 1517–1550 (Carnegie Institution of Washington, 1948).
Inga Clendinnen, Ambivalent Conquests: Maya and Spaniard in Yucatan, 1517–1570 (Cambridge University Press, 1987).
Peter Gerhard, The Southeast Frontier of New Spain, rev. ed. (University of Oklahoma Press, 1993).

properties.title: Valladolid founded among the Cupul
properties.label: Valladolid (Yucatán)
properties.description: Montejo's cousin, also named Francisco de Montejo, founded Valladolid in May 1543 at Chauac-Há near the coast to control the eastern Maya provinces. In March 1545 the settlers moved it inland to the Cupul town of Zací, beside a large cenote, where it became the main Spanish outpost in the east. In 1544 Gaspar Pacheco's campaign to the southeast set up Salamanca de Bacalar, near the bay of Chetumal.
properties.note: Marked at the second site (Zací, the modern city). The first site, Chauac-Há, lay in the present municipality of Tizimín. Sources give 23, 27 or 28 May 1543 for the founding.

sources.citation: Robert S. Chamberlain, The Conquest and Colonization of Yucatan, 1517–1550 (Carnegie Institution of Washington, 1948).
Peter Gerhard, The Southeast Frontier of New Spain, rev. ed. (University of Oklahoma Press, 1993).
Paul Gillingham, Mexico: A 500-Year History (Atlantic Monthly Press, 2025), ch. 3.

properties.title: The Great Maya Revolt in eastern Yucatán
properties.label: Maya revolt 1546
properties.description: On the night of 8 November 1546 the eastern provinces (the Cupul, Cochuah, Sotuta and others) rose together, killing Spanish encomenderos and hundreds of Maya servants of the Spaniards and besieging Valladolid. Spanish forces from Mérida and Campeche broke the rising after about four months. It was the last large coordinated Maya war against the conquest in the north, though the forested south and east stayed beyond Spanish control.
properties.note: The rising spread across the eastern provinces; the point marks the area around Valladolid, its main target.

sources.citation: Robert S. Chamberlain, The Conquest and Colonization of Yucatan, 1517–1550 (Carnegie Institution of Washington, 1948).
Inga Clendinnen, Ambivalent Conquests: Maya and Spaniard in Yucatan, 1517–1570 (Cambridge University Press, 1987).
Paul Gillingham, Mexico: A 500-Year History (Atlantic Monthly Press, 2025), ch. 5.

properties.title: Diego de Landa's auto de fe at Maní
properties.label: Maní 1562
properties.description: The discovery of idols and skulls in a cave near Maní led the Franciscans, under their provincial Diego de Landa, to interrogate Maya converts under torture across the region for three months; by Clendinnen's count some 4,500 were tortured and 158 died. The campaign ended in an auto de fe at Maní at which Maya books and thousands of images were burned. Landa was recalled to Spain to answer for it, and there wrote the Relación de las cosas de Yucatán, a key source on Maya culture.
properties.note: The number of books burned is not reliably known.

sources.citation: Inga Clendinnen, Ambivalent Conquests: Maya and Spaniard in Yucatan, 1517–1570 (Cambridge University Press, 1987).
Paul Gillingham, Mexico: A 500-Year History (Atlantic Monthly Press, 2025), ch. 3.

properties.title: Nuño de Guzmán's conquest of the west
properties.label: Guzmán 1529–31
properties.description: Nuño de Guzmán, president of the first audiencia, left Mexico City with several hundred Spaniards and thousands of Indigenous allies to conquer the lands beyond Michoacán. In Michoacán he tortured and burned the Tarascan ruler Tangáxuan II (February 1530); he then marched through Tonalá, the Caxcan country around Nochistlán, Tepic and the coast of Aztatlán, where a hurricane and floods in September 1530 killed many of his Indigenous auxiliaries, and on through Chiametla to Culiacán, enslaving and killing on a scale that depopulated much of the region. The brutality of the campaign is the background to the Mixtón War a decade later.
properties.note: Main stops only (Tzintzuntzan, the Lerma near Puruándiro, Tonalá, Nochistlán, Tepic, Chiametla marked at Escuinapa, Culiacán); the line between them is schematic. Guzmán also sent detachments in other directions.

sources.citation: Ida Altman, The War for Mexico's West: Indians and Spaniards in New Galicia, 1524–1550 (University of New Mexico Press, 2010).
Peter Gerhard, The North Frontier of New Spain, rev. ed. (University of Oklahoma Press, 1993).
Paul Gillingham, Mexico: A 500-Year History (Atlantic Monthly Press, 2025), chs. 2 and 5.

properties.title: San Miguel de Culiacán founded
properties.label: Culiacán
properties.description: The northernmost town of Guzmán's conquest, for decades an isolated outpost on the Pacific coastal plain. In 1536 Spanish slavers nearby met Álvar Núñez Cabeza de Vaca and his three companions, survivors of the Narváez expedition who had walked from the Texas coast; their stories of rich towns to the north led to the expeditions of Fray Marcos de Niza (1539) and Coronado (1540).
properties.note: The town was moved at least once in its early years; the point marks modern Culiacán.

sources.citation: Peter Gerhard, The North Frontier of New Spain, rev. ed. (University of Oklahoma Press, 1993).
Ida Altman, The War for Mexico's West: Indians and Spaniards in New Galicia, 1524–1550 (University of New Mexico Press, 2010).
Paul Gillingham, Mexico: A 500-Year History (Atlantic Monthly Press, 2025), ch. 1.

properties.title: The wandering city: Guadalajara's four sites
properties.label: Guadalajara's moves
properties.description: Guadalajara was founded by Cristóbal de Oñate for Guzmán at Nochistlán, then moved to Tonalá (1533) and to Tlacotán, north of the Río Grande de Santiago, before settling in the valley of Atemajac in 1542. The moves followed water, Indigenous resistance and Guzmán's orders, and the last came after the town had nearly been overrun in the Mixtón War.
properties.note: Each vertex is one site: Nochistlán, Tonalá, Tlacotán (marked at the modern village of that name) and Guadalajara. Sources differ on the dates of the first founding (January 1531 or January 1532) and of the move to Tlacotán (1535 or about 1537).

sources.citation: Ida Altman, The War for Mexico's West: Indians and Spaniards in New Galicia, 1524–1550 (University of New Mexico Press, 2010).
Peter Gerhard, The North Frontier of New Spain, rev. ed. (University of Oklahoma Press, 1993).

properties.title: Vasco de Quiroga in Michoacán
properties.label: Vasco de Quiroga
properties.description: Vasco de Quiroga, a judge of the second audiencia, founded "hospital-towns" of Santa Fe near Mexico City and on Lake Pátzcuaro in the early 1530s, inspired partly by Thomas More's Utopia. As the first bishop of Michoacán he fought the Augustinians and Franciscans for control of the diocese, most violently over a new Augustinian convent at Tlazazalca (1558–62); he moved the see from Tzintzuntzan to Pátzcuaro, gathered dispersed Purépecha communities into towns and, by tradition, encouraged each to specialise in a craft (copper at Santa Clara, lacquer at Uruapan), a pattern still visible in the region. The see moved to Valladolid in 1580.
properties.note: Marked at the Basílica de Nuestra Señora de la Salud, built as Quiroga's cathedral. Quiroga was appointed bishop in 1536 and consecrated in 1538, and the move to Pátzcuaro took place in 1538–40; he died in 1565. The craft-specialisation story is partly tradition. Gillingham (ch. 5) says Quiroga's men burned the Tlazazalca convent on 23 June 1560; the conflict there (1558–62) is confirmed by Cerdá Farías's study of the convent, but the burning was not checked independently.
properties.modern_place: Basílica de Nuestra Señora de la Salud, Pátzcuaro

sources.citation: Fintan B. Warren, Vasco de Quiroga and His Pueblo-Hospitals of Santa Fe (Academy of American Franciscan History, 1963).
Peter Gerhard, A Guide to the Historical Geography of New Spain, rev. ed. (University of Oklahoma Press, 1993).
Paul Gillingham, Mexico: A 500-Year History (Atlantic Monthly Press, 2025), chs. 3 and 5.

properties.title: Valladolid (Morelia) founded
properties.label: Valladolid (Morelia)
properties.description: Viceroy Antonio de Mendoza founded a Spanish city in the valley of Guayangareo, on the road from Mexico to Nueva Galicia, as a rival to Quiroga's Pátzcuaro. As Valladolid it took over the bishopric (1580) and the provincial government and became the capital of Michoacán; it was renamed Morelia in 1828.
properties.note: The founding is usually dated May 1541.

sources.citation: Peter Gerhard, A Guide to the Historical Geography of New Spain, rev. ed. (University of Oklahoma Press, 1993).
Fintan B. Warren, Vasco de Quiroga and His Pueblo-Hospitals of Santa Fe (Academy of American Franciscan History, 1963).

properties.title: Puebla de los Ángeles founded
properties.label: Puebla
properties.description: The second audiencia and the Franciscans founded Puebla as a town for Spaniards who would farm rather than live on Indigenous tribute, on unoccupied land between Cholula, Tlaxcala and Huejotzingo, with Indigenous labour from those towns. Placed halfway along the road from Veracruz to Mexico City, it grew into New Spain's second city, a centre of wheat, textiles and pottery, and the seat of the bishopric of Tlaxcala from 1543.
properties.note: The official founding date; the first site flooded and the town was soon re-laid out nearby.

sources.citation: Peter Gerhard, A Guide to the Historical Geography of New Spain, rev. ed. (University of Oklahoma Press, 1993).
Michael C. Meyer, William L. Sherman and Susan M. Deeds, The Course of Mexican History, 10th ed. (Oxford University Press, 2014).

properties.title: Querétaro, Otomí town on the frontier
properties.label: Querétaro
properties.description: Querétaro began as a town of Otomí allies of the Spaniards, led by the cacique Conín (baptised Fernando de Tapia), on the edge of the Chichimeca lands. With the opening of the Zacatecas road it became a key way-station and supply centre, and Spaniards settled there in growing numbers.
properties.note: The traditional founding date of 25 July 1531 is disputed; some historians place the founding about 1540.

sources.citation: Peter Gerhard, A Guide to the Historical Geography of New Spain, rev. ed. (University of Oklahoma Press, 1993).
Philip Wayne Powell, Soldiers, Indians, and Silver: The Northward Advance of New Spain, 1550–1600 (University of California Press, 1952).
Paul Gillingham, Mexico: A 500-Year History (Atlantic Monthly Press, 2025), chs. 1 and 6.

properties.title: Antequera (Oaxaca) made a city
properties.label: Antequera
properties.description: Spaniards under Francisco de Orozco occupied the Aztec garrison town of Huaxyacac in the Valley of Oaxaca in late 1521. Cortés, who wanted the valley for himself (it became the core of his Marquesado del Valle de Oaxaca), tried to suppress the Spanish town, but the Crown chartered it as the city of Antequera in 1532. It became the seat of a bishopric and the centre of the cochineal trade of the Mixtec and Zapotec highlands.

sources.citation: Peter Gerhard, A Guide to the Historical Geography of New Spain, rev. ed. (University of Oklahoma Press, 1993).

properties.title: Cuernavaca: Cortés's palace and the Marquesado del Valle
properties.label: Cortés's palace, Cuernavaca
properties.description: In 1529 Charles V made Cortés Marqués del Valle de Oaxaca, with lordship over some 23,000 Indigenous vassals in scattered blocks from the Valley of Mexico to Oaxaca, Tehuantepec and the Tuxtlas. Kept out of Mexico City for a time, he made his base at Cuernavaca, completing a fortified palace there by 1535, and his estates in the Tuxtlas and around Cuernavaca were among the first sugar plantations in New Spain. The marquisate survived, with interruptions, as a private lordship to the end of colonial rule.
properties.note: Marked at the Palacio de Cortés. Sources give 2, 6 or 20 July 1529 for the grant; the span ends with Cortés's death in Spain in 1547.

sources.citation: Bernardo García Martínez, El Marquesado del Valle: tres siglos de régimen señorial en Nueva España (El Colegio de México, 1969).
Instituto Nacional de Antropología e Historia (INAH), "Museo Regional Cuauhnáhuac, Palacio de Cortés" (site page).
Peter Gerhard, A Guide to the Historical Geography of New Spain, rev. ed. (University of Oklahoma Press, 1993).
Paul Gillingham, Mexico: A 500-Year History (Atlantic Monthly Press, 2025), chs. 2, 5 and 6.

properties.title: Taxco silver mines
properties.label: Taxco
properties.description: Among the first silver mines worked by Spaniards in New Spain, along with Sultepec and Zumpango, in the mountains south of the capital. These early mines, worked by enslaved and drafted Indigenous labour, were small beside the northern strikes that came after 1546.
properties.note: Mining began around 1534; the first workings were at Taxco el Viejo, south of the present town.

sources.citation: Peter Gerhard, A Guide to the Historical Geography of New Spain, rev. ed. (University of Oklahoma Press, 1993).
Peter Bakewell, "Mining in colonial Spanish America", in Leslie Bethell (ed.), The Cambridge History of Latin America, vol. 2 (Cambridge University Press, 1984).

properties.title: First viceroy: Antonio de Mendoza
properties.label: Viceroyalty 1535
properties.description: To curb the conquistadors and the first audiencia's abuses, the Crown made New Spain a viceroyalty and sent Antonio de Mendoza, who arrived in 1535 and governed for fifteen years. He set up the institutions of colonial rule, the mint (1535) and the printing press (1539), sent Coronado north, and crushed the Mixtón rising in person. The viceroy ruled from the palace that Cortés had built on the site of Moctezuma's palace.
properties.note: Marked at the Palacio Nacional, the former viceregal palace (acquired by the Crown from Cortés's heirs in 1562).

sources.citation: Michael C. Meyer, William L. Sherman and Susan M. Deeds, The Course of Mexican History, 10th ed. (Oxford University Press, 2014).
Charles Gibson, The Aztecs under Spanish Rule: A History of the Indians of the Valley of Mexico, 1519–1810 (Stanford University Press, 1964).
Paul Gillingham, Mexico: A 500-Year History (Atlantic Monthly Press, 2025), chs. 2 and 5.

properties.title: Colegio de Santa Cruz de Tlatelolco
properties.description: The Franciscans opened a college at Tlatelolco to teach Latin, rhetoric and theology to the sons of the Nahua nobility, meant as the core of an Indigenous clergy and elite. Indians were soon barred from the priesthood, so it never produced the clergy hoped for, but its graduates and teachers worked with Fray Bernardino de Sahagún on the Florentine Codex and with other friars on Nahuatl grammars and texts, and it had one of the first libraries in the Americas.
properties.note: Marked at the church of Santiago Tlatelolco, beside which the college stood.
properties.modern_place: Templo de Santiago Tlatelolco, Ciudad de México

sources.citation: Robert Ricard, The Spiritual Conquest of Mexico: An Essay on the Apostolate and the Evangelizing Methods of the Mendicant Orders in New Spain, 1523–1572, trans. Lesley Byrd Simpson (University of California Press, 1966).
Barbara E. Mundy, The Death of Aztec Tenochtitlan, the Life of Mexico City (University of Texas Press, 2015).
Paul Gillingham, Mexico: A 500-Year History (Atlantic Monthly Press, 2025), chs. 3 and 6.

properties.title: Tepeyac: the shrine of Guadalupe
properties.label: Tepeyac (Guadalupe)
properties.description: On the hill of Tepeyac, at the northern end of the causeway to the island city and, according to Sahagún, once a shrine of the mother goddess Tonantzin, a chapel of the Virgin of Guadalupe was drawing Indigenous and Spanish pilgrims by the 1550s. In 1556 Archbishop Montúfar promoted its image while the Franciscan provincial, Francisco de Bustamante, attacked the cult from the pulpit as idolatry around a recent picture painted by an Indian. The story that the Virgin appeared to Juan Diego here in December 1531 was first published only in 1648–49, after which Guadalupe grew into the national symbol of Mexico.
properties.note: Marked at the modern basilica; the sixteenth-century chapel stood at the foot of the hill nearby. Whether the 1531 apparitions happened is a matter of faith; the earliest documents mention the chapel and its miracles but not the apparitions.
properties.modern_place: Basílica de Santa María de Guadalupe, Ciudad de México

sources.citation: Stafford Poole, Our Lady of Guadalupe: The Origins and Sources of a Mexican National Symbol, 1531–1797 (University of Arizona Press, 1995).
Paul Gillingham, Mexico: A 500-Year History (Atlantic Monthly Press, 2025), ch. 3.

properties.title: Cortés in California: Santa Cruz
properties.label: Santa Cruz 1535
properties.description: Cortés, now Marqués del Valle but shut out of government, spent his fortune on Pacific voyages from the shipyards of the west coast. In May 1535 he landed on the Bay of La Paz and founded a colony called Santa Cruz, abandoned within about a year for lack of food. In 1539–40 his captain Francisco de Ulloa sailed to the head of the Gulf of California and showed that "California" was a peninsula, though later maps often drew it as an island.
properties.note: Marked at La Paz; the colony stood on the shore of the bay.
properties.modern_place: La Paz, Baja California Sur, Mexico

sources.citation: Henry R. Wagner, Spanish Voyages to the Northwest Coast of America in the Sixteenth Century (California Historical Society, 1929).
Peter Gerhard, The North Frontier of New Spain, rev. ed. (University of Oklahoma Press, 1993).
Paul Gillingham, Mexico: A 500-Year History (Atlantic Monthly Press, 2025), ch. 2.

properties.title: Coronado's expedition to Cíbola and Quivira
properties.label: Coronado 1540–42
properties.description: Drawn by Fray Marcos de Niza's report of the "Seven Cities of Cíbola", Francisco Vázquez de Coronado, governor of Nueva Galicia, led some 350 Spaniards and 1,300 or more Indigenous allies from Compostela up the Pacific slope to Culiacán and the Sonora valley, across southeastern Arizona to the Zuni pueblos, and on to the Rio Grande pueblos of Tiguex, where they spent two winters and fought the Tiguex War. In 1541 a party crossed the Llano Estacado to Quivira, the grass-house villages of the Wichita in central Kansas. They found no gold, and the failure left the far north alone until the 1580s.
properties.note: The outward route only, after the Flints' and Bolton's reconstructions: Compostela, Culiacán, the Río Mayo (schematic), Corazones (marked at Ures), Arizpe, the San Pedro valley (Coronado National Memorial), Chichilticale (schematic, in the Sulphur Springs Valley), Hawikuh, Acoma, Tiguex (Kuaua), Pecos, Blanco Canyon (Floydada) and Quivira (Lyons, Kansas). Several stops are debated.

sources.citation: Richard Flint and Shirley Cushing Flint (eds. and trans.), Documents of the Coronado Expedition, 1539–1542 (Southern Methodist University Press, 2005).
Herbert E. Bolton, Coronado: Knight of Pueblos and Plains (Whittlesey House / University of New Mexico Press, 1949).
Paul Gillingham, Mexico: A 500-Year History (Atlantic Monthly Press, 2025), ch. 2.

properties.title: Coronado takes Hawikuh (Cíbola)
properties.label: Hawikuh
properties.description: At the Zuni pueblo of Hawikuh, the first of the "cities of Cíbola", the hungry expedition stormed the town when its people refused entry, and Coronado was badly hurt in the assault. The stone and adobe villages were nothing like Fray Marcos's description, and the expedition turned east toward the Rio Grande.
properties.note: Coordinates of the Hawikuh ruins from Wikipedia. The geocoder check uses Zuni Pueblo, about 20 km to the northeast, so a distance of that size is expected. Usually dated 7 July 1540.

sources.citation: Richard Flint and Shirley Cushing Flint (eds. and trans.), Documents of the Coronado Expedition, 1539–1542 (Southern Methodist University Press, 2005).
Herbert E. Bolton, Coronado: Knight of Pueblos and Plains (Whittlesey House / University of New Mexico Press, 1949).

properties.title: Mixtón War: the Caxcan rising
properties.label: Mixtón
properties.description: Caxcan, Zacateco and other peoples of Nueva Galicia, worn down by Guzmán's conquest and the encomenderos who followed, rose in 1540 and fortified themselves on steep peñoles (rock strongholds) such as Mixtón and Nochistlán, led by Tenamaxtli of Nochistlán among others. The rising threatened to sweep the Spaniards out of the west, and Viceroy Mendoza himself took a large army, mostly Indigenous allies from central Mexico, to put it down in 1541–42. The fall of Mixtón ended the war, and many captives were enslaved.
properties.note: The Mixtón peñol has not been securely located; it lay in the hills of the Juchipila valley. The point marks Apozol, near where tradition places it. Gillingham (chs. 1 and 3) stresses the religious character of the rising, whose leaders promised victory through their god Tecoroli, and gives Mendoza's army as some 30,000 central Mexican allies.

sources.citation: Ida Altman, The War for Mexico's West: Indians and Spaniards in New Galicia, 1524–1550 (University of New Mexico Press, 2010).
Peter Gerhard, The North Frontier of New Spain, rev. ed. (University of Oklahoma Press, 1993).
Paul Gillingham, Mexico: A 500-Year History (Atlantic Monthly Press, 2025), chs. 1, 3 and 5.

properties.title: Pedro de Alvarado mortally injured
properties.label: Alvarado's death
properties.description: Pedro de Alvarado, the conqueror of Guatemala, was in Nueva Galicia with a fleet he had built for a Pacific expedition when he joined the war. Refusing to wait for reinforcements, he attacked the rebels on their peñol, was driven back, and in the retreat was crushed when a horse fell on him. He died at Guadalajara on 4 July 1541.
properties.note: Most accounts place the attack at the peñol of Nochistlán; some place it at Mixtón. Marked at Nochistlán.

sources.citation: Ida Altman, The War for Mexico's West: Indians and Spaniards in New Galicia, 1524–1550 (University of New Mexico Press, 2010).
Paul Gillingham, Mexico: A 500-Year History (Atlantic Monthly Press, 2025), ch. 1.

properties.title: Attack on Guadalajara (Tlacotán)
properties.label: Guadalajara attacked
properties.description: Emboldened by Alvarado's defeat, the rebels attacked Guadalajara, then at its third site at Tlacotán, and were driven off by its small garrison. Viceroy Mendoza's army arrived that autumn, took Nochistlán in November and Mixtón in the following months, and in February 1542 the town was moved to the safer valley of Atemajac.
properties.note: Marked at the village of Tlacotán, Ixtlahuacán del Río; the colonial site is nearby.

sources.citation: Ida Altman, The War for Mexico's West: Indians and Spaniards in New Galicia, 1524–1550 (University of New Mexico Press, 2010).
Paul Gillingham, Mexico: A 500-Year History (Atlantic Monthly Press, 2025), ch. 5.

properties.title: Guadalajara at its present site
properties.label: Guadalajara
properties.description: The fourth and final site of Guadalajara, in the valley of Atemajac. In 1560 the audiencia and bishopric of Nueva Galicia moved here from Compostela, making Guadalajara the capital of the west and, in time, Mexico's second city.

sources.citation: Ida Altman, The War for Mexico's West: Indians and Spaniards in New Galicia, 1524–1550 (University of New Mexico Press, 2010).
Peter Gerhard, The North Frontier of New Spain, rev. ed. (University of Oklahoma Press, 1993).

properties.title: Audiencia of Nueva Galicia established at Compostela
properties.label: Audiencia of Nueva Galicia
properties.description: The Crown created a separate audiencia (high court and governing council) for Nueva Galicia in 1548, seated at Compostela, a small town near the Pacific founded by Guzmán's men in 1531–32. With the silver of Zacatecas in its district, it moved to Guadalajara in 1560. The audiencia gave the west a measure of autonomy from Mexico City that it kept for the rest of the colonial period.
properties.note: Compostela was first founded near Tepic and moved to its present site about 1540; the point marks the present town. Coronado mustered his expedition here in February 1540.

sources.citation: Peter Gerhard, The North Frontier of New Spain, rev. ed. (University of Oklahoma Press, 1993).
Ida Altman, The War for Mexico's West: Indians and Spaniards in New Galicia, 1524–1550 (University of New Mexico Press, 2010).

properties.title: Silver at Zacatecas
properties.label: Zacatecas silver
properties.description: In September 1546 a party led by Juan de Tolosa reached the Cerro de la Bufa and found silver-bearing ore; rich veins such as San Bernabé were found in 1548, and Tolosa, Cristóbal de Oñate, Diego de Ibarra and Baltasar Temiño de Bañuelos became the founders of the town. Zacatecas quickly became the richest mining district in New Spain, pulling Spanish settlement, roads, livestock and labour hundreds of kilometres north into the lands of the Chichimecas.

sources.citation: P. J. Bakewell, Silver Mining and Society in Colonial Mexico: Zacatecas 1546–1700 (Cambridge University Press, 1971).
Philip Wayne Powell, Soldiers, Indians, and Silver: The Northward Advance of New Spain, 1550–1600 (University of California Press, 1952).
Paul Gillingham, Mexico: A 500-Year History (Atlantic Monthly Press, 2025), chs. 3 and 6.

properties.title: Silver at Guanajuato
properties.label: Guanajuato silver
properties.description: Prospectors and muleteers on the Zacatecas road found silver in the ravines of the Sierra de Guanajuato from about 1548, and in the 1550s the great Veta Madre (Mother Lode) was opened at Rayas and Mellado. Guanajuato grew into one of the two great mining centres of New Spain, and its mines and the farms that fed them filled the Bajío with Spanish, mestizo and Indigenous settlers.
properties.note: Dates for the first strikes vary between 1548 and the mid-1550s. The mining camp (real de minas) dates from about 1554, the town was legally constituted about 1570, and it became a villa only in 1679. Gillingham (ch. 6) dates the Guanajuato discovery to 1550.

sources.citation: Peter Bakewell, "Mining in colonial Spanish America", in Leslie Bethell (ed.), The Cambridge History of Latin America, vol. 2 (Cambridge University Press, 1984).
Peter Gerhard, A Guide to the Historical Geography of New Spain, rev. ed. (University of Oklahoma Press, 1993).
Philip Wayne Powell, Soldiers, Indians, and Silver: The Northward Advance of New Spain, 1550–1600 (University of California Press, 1952).
Paul Gillingham, Mexico: A 500-Year History (Atlantic Monthly Press, 2025), ch. 6.

properties.title: Pachuca: the patio process
properties.label: Patio process
properties.description: At a refining works in Pachuca, Bartolomé de Medina perfected the patio process, in which crushed silver ore was mixed with mercury, salt and copper sulphate in large open courtyards. It made low-grade ores profitable and spread to every major mine in the Americas, making the silver economy dependent on mercury shipped from Almadén in Spain and later Huancavelica in Peru.
properties.note: Medina is usually said to have developed the method in 1554–55; the exact hacienda is not located here. Gillingham (ch. 6) says Medina learned the method in Spain in 1553 before experimenting at Pachuca.

sources.citation: Peter Bakewell, "Mining in colonial Spanish America", in Leslie Bethell (ed.), The Cambridge History of Latin America, vol. 2 (Cambridge University Press, 1984).
P. J. Bakewell, Silver Mining and Society in Colonial Mexico: Zacatecas 1546–1700 (Cambridge University Press, 1971).
Paul Gillingham, Mexico: A 500-Year History (Atlantic Monthly Press, 2025), ch. 6.

properties.title: Sheep in the Valle del Mezquital
properties.label: Valle del Mezquital
properties.description: Spanish sheep, introduced on a large scale under Viceroy Mendoza, multiplied explosively in the Otomí country of the Valle del Mezquital north of Mexico City, where grazing rules let flocks roam over unfenced Indigenous fields. Melville argues that by the 1590s overgrazing, together with the epidemics, had turned a fertile farming valley into mesquite scrub. Africans working as herdsmen and overseers were, on her figures, the largest group of newcomers in the valley.
properties.note: Marked at Ixmiquilpan, at the heart of the valley; the grazing region covered much of western Hidalgo. Melville's thesis of a man-made degradation is influential but has been questioned by other environmental historians.

sources.citation: Elinor G. K. Melville, A Plague of Sheep: Environmental Consequences of the Conquest of Mexico (Cambridge University Press, 1994).
Paul Gillingham, Mexico: A 500-Year History (Atlantic Monthly Press, 2025), chs. 2 and 3.

properties.title: Fresnillo
properties.label: Fresnillo
properties.description: Francisco de Ibarra's expedition reached a spring at Fresnillo in September 1554, near the Cerro de Proaño where ore had been found a few years before. Fresnillo was one of a string of mining camps (with Sombrerete, Chalchihuites and San Martín) opened north and west of Zacatecas in the 1550s.

sources.citation: P. J. Bakewell, Silver Mining and Society in Colonial Mexico: Zacatecas 1546–1700 (Cambridge University Press, 1971).
J. Lloyd Mecham, Francisco de Ibarra and Nueva Vizcaya (Duke University Press, 1927).

properties.title: Sombrerete
properties.label: Sombrerete
properties.description: Silver deposits found in the mid-1550s, by tradition by Juan de Tolosa, made Sombrerete one of the richest northern camps. It lay on the road northwest from Zacatecas toward Durango.

sources.citation: P. J. Bakewell, Silver Mining and Society in Colonial Mexico: Zacatecas 1546–1700 (Cambridge University Press, 1971).
Peter Gerhard, The North Frontier of New Spain, rev. ed. (University of Oklahoma Press, 1993).

properties.title: Camino Real de Tierra Adentro (the silver road)
properties.label: Camino Real
properties.description: The royal road north from Mexico City grew out of the cart road opened to Zacatecas around 1550, and was for a time the longest road in North America. It carried mercury, tools, cloth and food north and silver south, and it was the main target of Chichimeca raids. As mining moved north it was extended to Durango and Santa Bárbara, and in 1598 Oñate carried it to New Mexico, making it a road of some 2,500 km.
properties.note: Drawn through documented stops: Cuautitlán, Tepeji, San Juan del Río, Querétaro, San Miguel, San Felipe, Ojuelos, Aguascalientes (founded 1575 as a waystation), Zacatecas, Fresnillo, Sombrerete, Nombre de Dios, Durango, Indé and Santa Bárbara. The road shifted over time and had branches (e.g. via Celaya and León); the section north of Durango is schematic.

sources.citation: Philip Wayne Powell, Soldiers, Indians, and Silver: The Northward Advance of New Spain, 1550–1600 (University of California Press, 1952).
US National Park Service, El Camino Real de Tierra Adentro National Historic Trail, "History & Culture".
Peter Gerhard, The North Frontier of New Spain, rev. ed. (University of Oklahoma Press, 1993).
Paul Gillingham, Mexico: A 500-Year History (Atlantic Monthly Press, 2025), chs. 3 and 6.

properties.title: San Miguel el Grande: a defended town on the road
properties.label: San Miguel
properties.description: A Franciscan mission settlement of the 1540s was refounded in 1555 as a Spanish villa to guard the Zacatecas road against Chichimeca raids. It was the first of a chain of defensive towns and forts (presidios) placed along the road; it later became San Miguel de Allende.
properties.modern_place: San Miguel de Allende, Guanajuato, Mexico

sources.citation: Philip Wayne Powell, Soldiers, Indians, and Silver: The Northward Advance of New Spain, 1550–1600 (University of California Press, 1952).
Peter Gerhard, A Guide to the Historical Geography of New Spain, rev. ed. (University of Oklahoma Press, 1993).
Paul Gillingham, Mexico: A 500-Year History (Atlantic Monthly Press, 2025), ch. 6.

properties.title: San Felipe: fort and town
properties.label: San Felipe
properties.description: Founded by Viceroy Luis de Velasco in 1562 at a dangerous stretch of the road between San Miguel and Ojuelos, as a garrisoned settlement of Spaniards and Indigenous allies. Like Celaya (1571), León (1576) and Aguascalientes (1575), it combined a fort with farmland, turning a war frontier into a settled one.

sources.citation: Philip Wayne Powell, Soldiers, Indians, and Silver: The Northward Advance of New Spain, 1550–1600 (University of California Press, 1952).

properties.title: Celaya founded
properties.description: Viceroy Martín Enríquez licensed a villa of Spanish farmers at Celaya, on the plain of the Laja river in the Bajío, to guard the roads to Zacatecas and Guanajuato and to grow grain for the mines. With León, Aguascalientes and San Felipe it was one of the farming and garrison towns that turned the Bajío from a war frontier into the granary of the silver economy.
properties.note: The viceroy's licence is dated 12 October 1570; the town council was set up on 1 January 1571, the date shown.

sources.citation: Philip Wayne Powell, Soldiers, Indians, and Silver: The Northward Advance of New Spain, 1550–1600 (University of California Press, 1952).
Peter Gerhard, A Guide to the Historical Geography of New Spain, rev. ed. (University of Oklahoma Press, 1993).
Paul Gillingham, Mexico: A 500-Year History (Atlantic Monthly Press, 2025), ch. 6.

properties.title: León founded
properties.description: On the viceroy's orders Juan Bautista de Orozco founded the Villa de León in the valley of Señora, at the western end of the Bajío, as a defended settlement of Spanish farmers and ranchers against Chichimeca raids on the roads between Guanajuato, Zacatecas and Nueva Galicia. It became the centre of a rich farming and livestock district.
properties.note: Gillingham (ch. 6) dates León to 1585; the founding of 20 January 1576 is the usual date.
properties.modern_place: León de los Aldama, Guanajuato, Mexico

sources.citation: Philip Wayne Powell, Soldiers, Indians, and Silver: The Northward Advance of New Spain, 1550–1600 (University of California Press, 1952).
Peter Gerhard, A Guide to the Historical Geography of New Spain, rev. ed. (University of Oklahoma Press, 1993).
Paul Gillingham, Mexico: A 500-Year History (Atlantic Monthly Press, 2025), ch. 6.

properties.title: Durango (Guadiana), capital of Nueva Vizcaya
properties.label: Durango
properties.description: Francisco de Ibarra, nephew of one of the founders of Zacatecas, was made governor of the new province of Nueva Vizcaya in 1562 and founded the Villa de Durango as its capital the next year. Nueva Vizcaya, covering the modern states of Durango and Chihuahua and at first parts of Sinaloa and Sonora, became the main northern province beyond Nueva Galicia.

sources.citation: J. Lloyd Mecham, Francisco de Ibarra and Nueva Vizcaya (Duke University Press, 1927).
Peter Gerhard, The North Frontier of New Spain, rev. ed. (University of Oklahoma Press, 1993).

properties.title: Santa Bárbara
properties.label: Santa Bárbara
properties.description: A mining camp founded by Rodrigo del Río de Loza in the headwaters of the Río Conchos, for decades the northernmost Spanish settlement on the mainland. Expeditions to New Mexico (Rodríguez–Chamuscado 1581, Espejo 1582 and Oñate 1598) set out from here or the nearby valley of San Bartolomé.

sources.citation: Robert C. West, The Mining Community in Northern New Spain: The Parral Mining District (University of California Press, 1949).
Peter Gerhard, The North Frontier of New Spain, rev. ed. (University of Oklahoma Press, 1993).
Paul Gillingham, Mexico: A 500-Year History (Atlantic Monthly Press, 2025), chs. 1 and 6.

properties.title: Aguascalientes founded
properties.description: The audiencia of Nueva Galicia licensed Juan de Montoro and about a dozen settlers from Lagos to found the Villa de Nuestra Señora de la Asunción de las Aguas Calientes at hot springs on the road between Guadalajara, Mexico City and Zacatecas. It was a small fortified waystation in Chichimeca country, almost deserted in its early years, and grew only after the peace of the 1590s.
properties.note: The date is that of the founding licence. Gillingham (chs. 1, 6 and 7) treats it as a typical supply town of the silver road; he dates its refounding, with a grid plan and the Indigenous barrio of San Marcos, to 1609.

sources.citation: Peter Gerhard, The North Frontier of New Spain, rev. ed. (University of Oklahoma Press, 1993).
Philip Wayne Powell, Soldiers, Indians, and Silver: The Northward Advance of New Spain, 1550–1600 (University of California Press, 1952).
Paul Gillingham, Mexico: A 500-Year History (Atlantic Monthly Press, 2025), chs. 1, 6 and 7.

properties.title: Saltillo founded
properties.label: Saltillo
properties.description: Alberto del Canto founded the Villa de Santiago del Saltillo on the plateau east of the Sierra Madre, a waystation on the route from Zacatecas to the northeast. It became the gateway to Coahuila, Nuevo León and later Texas.
properties.note: Some sources give 1575.

sources.citation: Peter Gerhard, The North Frontier of New Spain, rev. ed. (University of Oklahoma Press, 1993).
Paul Gillingham, Mexico: A 500-Year History (Atlantic Monthly Press, 2025), ch. 6.

properties.title: Tlaxcalan colonists: San Esteban de Nueva Tlaxcala
properties.label: Tlaxcalan colonies 1591
properties.description: As part of the peace with the Chichimecas, Viceroy Luis de Velasco the younger negotiated with Tlaxcala to send about 400 families north as settlers and models of Christian farming life, with privileges such as noble status and exemption from tribute. They founded colonies beside Spanish and Chichimeca towns, among them San Esteban de Nueva Tlaxcala next to Saltillo and San Luis de Colotlán in Nueva Galicia, and Tlaxcalans later spread from these to settle much of the northeast.
properties.note: Marked at the church of San Esteban in Saltillo, the centre of the Tlaxcalan town, which stood beside the Spanish villa. Sources disagree on whether there were six or eight original colonies and on how the families were divided.

sources.citation: Philip Wayne Powell, Soldiers, Indians, and Silver: The Northward Advance of New Spain, 1550–1600 (University of California Press, 1952).
Peter Gerhard, The North Frontier of New Spain, rev. ed. (University of Oklahoma Press, 1993).
Paul Gillingham, Mexico: A 500-Year History (Atlantic Monthly Press, 2025), ch. 1.

properties.title: San Luis Potosí: silver at Cerro de San Pedro
properties.label: San Luis Potosí
properties.description: Silver was found at Cerro de San Pedro in early 1592 in the heart of Guachichil country, made possible by the peace that the mestizo captain Miguel Caldera had negotiated. Lacking water at the mines, the refining town was founded in the valley below as San Luis Minas del Potosí, named after the great Bolivian mine. Its quick growth, with Tlaxcalan and Chichimeca barrios, marked the end of the Chichimeca War.
properties.note: The date is the formal founding of the town; the mines lie about 20 km to the east.
properties.modern_place: San Luis Potosí, San Luis Potosí, Mexico

sources.citation: Philip Wayne Powell, Mexico's Miguel Caldera: The Taming of America's First Frontier, 1548–1597 (University of Arizona Press, 1977).
Philip Wayne Powell, Soldiers, Indians, and Silver: The Northward Advance of New Spain, 1550–1600 (University of California Press, 1952).

properties.title: Monterrey founded
properties.label: Monterrey
properties.description: Diego de Montemayor founded the Ciudad Metropolitana de Nuestra Señora de Monterrey at the springs of Santa Lucía, refounding the earlier settlements of Luis de Carvajal, a slave raider as much as a colonist, whose Nuevo Reino de León (granted 1579) had collapsed after his arrest by the Inquisition, which later burned several of his relatives as Judaizers. It remained a small frontier town until the eighteenth century.

sources.citation: Peter Gerhard, The North Frontier of New Spain, rev. ed. (University of Oklahoma Press, 1993).
Paul Gillingham, Mexico: A 500-Year History (Atlantic Monthly Press, 2025), ch. 7.

properties.title: Jesuit missions begin in Sinaloa
properties.label: Jesuits in Sinaloa
properties.description: The Jesuits Gonzalo de Tapia and Martín Pérez arrived at the small Spanish villa of San Felipe y Santiago de Sinaloa and began the mission system that, over the next century, spread north up the river valleys of Sinaloa and Sonora. Tapia was killed in 1594. The missions, rather than towns or mines, became the main instrument of Spanish expansion in the northwest.

sources.citation: Andrés Pérez de Ribas, History of the Triumphs of Our Holy Faith amongst the Most Barbarous and Fierce Peoples of the New World (1645), trans. Daniel T. Reff, Maureen Ahern and Richard K. Danford (University of Arizona Press, 1999).
Susan M. Deeds, Defiance and Deference in Mexico's Colonial North: Indians under Spanish Rule in Nueva Vizcaya (University of Texas Press, 2003).
Peter Gerhard, The North Frontier of New Spain, rev. ed. (University of Oklahoma Press, 1993).

properties.title: Oñate's entrada to New Mexico
properties.label: Oñate 1598
properties.description: Juan de Oñate, son of a founder of Zacatecas and married to a descendant of Cortés and Moctezuma, led about 130 soldiers with families, Franciscans, Indigenous servants, wagons and thousands of animals north from the Conchos valley. They crossed the desert to the Rio Grande below El Paso, went upriver through the Jornada del Muerto, and reached the pueblo of Ohkay Owingeh in July. The route became the northern section of the Camino Real.
properties.note: Main stops: the valley of San Bartolomé, the Chihuahua area (schematic), the Samalayuca dunes, La Toma (San Elizario), the ford at El Paso, Socorro, Santo Domingo and Ohkay Owingeh. The expedition left the Conchos camp in early 1598 (sources give January to March).

sources.citation: George P. Hammond and Agapito Rey (eds.), Don Juan de Oñate, Colonizer of New Mexico, 1595–1628 (University of New Mexico Press, 1953).
US National Park Service, El Camino Real de Tierra Adentro National Historic Trail, "History & Culture".
John L. Kessell, Spain in the Southwest: A Narrative History of Colonial New Mexico, Arizona, Texas, and California (University of Oklahoma Press, 2002).

properties.title: La Toma: Oñate claims New Mexico
properties.label: La Toma
properties.description: On the bank of the Rio Grande below the pass of El Paso, Oñate formally took possession of New Mexico and all its lands for the king. The expedition crossed the river at the pass a few days later.
properties.note: The ceremony is placed near San Elizario, Texas; the exact spot is not known.

sources.citation: George P. Hammond and Agapito Rey (eds.), Don Juan de Oñate, Colonizer of New Mexico, 1595–1628 (University of New Mexico Press, 1953).
John L. Kessell, Spain in the Southwest: A Narrative History of Colonial New Mexico, Arizona, Texas, and California (University of Oklahoma Press, 2002).

properties.title: San Juan de los Caballeros, first capital of New Mexico
properties.label: San Juan de los Caballeros
properties.description: Oñate set up his headquarters at the Tewa pueblo of Ohkay Owingeh, which the Spaniards renamed San Juan de los Caballeros, and soon moved across the river to Yunque Owingeh (San Gabriel). Spanish New Mexico was an isolated colony some 1,500 km beyond Zacatecas, supplied by wagon trains every few years.

sources.citation: George P. Hammond and Agapito Rey (eds.), Don Juan de Oñate, Colonizer of New Mexico, 1595–1628 (University of New Mexico Press, 1953).
US National Park Service, El Camino Real de Tierra Adentro National Historic Trail, "History & Culture".
John L. Kessell, Spain in the Southwest: A Narrative History of Colonial New Mexico, Arizona, Texas, and California (University of Oklahoma Press, 2002).

properties.title: Destruction of Acoma Pueblo
properties.label: Acoma 1599
properties.description: After the people of Acoma killed Juan de Zaldívar and other soldiers who had come demanding food in December 1598, Oñate sent Vicente de Zaldívar to punish the mesa-top pueblo. In three days of fighting the Spaniards took the mesa and killed several hundred people. Oñate sentenced the survivors to twenty years of servitude, and men over twenty-five to the loss of a foot. He was later tried and convicted in Mexico for his conduct in New Mexico.
properties.note: Casualty figures vary from about 500 to 800 or more. Whether the amputations were all carried out is debated.

sources.citation: George P. Hammond and Agapito Rey (eds.), Don Juan de Oñate, Colonizer of New Mexico, 1595–1628 (University of New Mexico Press, 1953).
John L. Kessell, Spain in the Southwest: A Narrative History of Colonial New Mexico, Arizona, Texas, and California (University of Oklahoma Press, 2002).
David J. Weber, The Spanish Frontier in North America (Yale University Press, 1992).
Paul Gillingham, Mexico: A 500-Year History (Atlantic Monthly Press, 2025), ch. 7.

properties.title: San Juan de Ulúa: the fleet port and Hawkins's defeat
properties.label: San Juan de Ulúa 1568
properties.description: By the 1560s convoys (flotas) sailed from Seville to San Juan de Ulúa, the only sheltered anchorage on the coast, and returned with silver. In September 1568 the English slave-trader John Hawkins, sheltering there with damaged ships, was attacked by the incoming fleet carrying the new viceroy, Martín Enríquez; only Hawkins's and Francis Drake's ships escaped. The episode started decades of English raiding against Spanish America and led to the fortification of the island.

sources.citation: Harry Kelsey, Sir John Hawkins: Queen Elizabeth's Slave Trader (Yale University Press, 2003).
Peter Gerhard, A Guide to the Historical Geography of New Spain, rev. ed. (University of Oklahoma Press, 1993).
Paul Gillingham, Mexico: A 500-Year History (Atlantic Monthly Press, 2025), ch. 6.

properties.title: The Ávila–Cortés conspiracy
properties.label: Conspiracy of 1566
properties.description: In July 1566 the audiencia arrested Martín Cortés, second Marqués del Valle, his half-brothers and young creole friends, accused of plotting to kill the royal officials and make the marquis king of an independent New Spain, angered by the Crown's moves to stop encomiendas passing to further generations. On 3 August the brothers Alonso de Ávila Alvarado and Gil González de Ávila were beheaded in the plaza and their houses beside the ruins of the Templo Mayor were demolished, with a stone slab recording their crime set up on the site. A royal inquiry in 1567–68 executed and tortured more suspects, among them Malintzin's son Martín; the episode ended the political power of the conquistadors' heirs.
properties.note: Marked at the site of the Ávila houses (the corner of the modern streets of Guatemala and Argentina, beside the Templo Mayor). Whether there was a real plot is doubted. Gillingham (ch. 5) says two Spaniards were hanged; the Ávila brothers were in fact beheaded.
properties.modern_place: Templo Mayor, Ciudad de México, Mexico

sources.citation: Gabriela Sánchez Reyes, "El padrón de Alonso de Ávila Alvarado de 1567 y el templo de Huitzilopochtli", Boletín de Monumentos Históricos, tercera época, 41 (2017).
Paul Gillingham, Mexico: A 500-Year History (Atlantic Monthly Press, 2025), ch. 5.

properties.title: Legazpi sails for the Philippines
properties.label: Navidad 1564
properties.description: Miguel López de Legazpi's expedition sailed from the port of Navidad on the coast of Nueva Galicia with Andrés de Urdaneta, an Augustinian friar and veteran navigator, as pilot. Legazpi founded the first Spanish settlement in the Philippines at Cebu (1565) and Manila in 1571, which became the Asian end of the galleon trade.

sources.citation: William Lytle Schurz, The Manila Galleon (E. P. Dutton, 1939).
Arturo Giráldez, The Age of Trade: The Manila Galleons and the Dawn of the Global Economy (Rowman & Littlefield, 2015).
Paul Gillingham, Mexico: A 500-Year History (Atlantic Monthly Press, 2025), ch. 5.

properties.title: Acapulco, terminus of the Manila galleon
properties.label: Acapulco
properties.description: The San Pedro, with Urdaneta aboard, reached Acapulco on 8 October 1565 after finding a way back across the Pacific. Acapulco's deep, sheltered bay, closer to Mexico City than any other Pacific port, made it the American terminus of the galleons, which brought Chinese silk, porcelain and other Asian goods in exchange for Mexican and Peruvian silver. From 1593 the trade was restricted to two ships a year.

sources.citation: William Lytle Schurz, The Manila Galleon (E. P. Dutton, 1939).
Arturo Giráldez, The Age of Trade: The Manila Galleons and the Dawn of the Global Economy (Rowman & Littlefield, 2015).
Paul Gillingham, Mexico: A 500-Year History (Atlantic Monthly Press, 2025), ch. 6.

properties.title: Manila galleon: westbound route to Manila
properties.label: Galleon to Manila
properties.description: Leaving Acapulco in late winter or spring, the galleons sailed southwest to the trade-wind belt and ran west at low latitudes to Guam and on to Manila, a voyage of about three months with the wind behind them. The route made New Spain the link between Spain's Atlantic empire and Asia.
properties.note: Schematic: the westbound track ran roughly between 10° and 14°N but varied by voyage. The line stops at 130°W, the western edge of the map; Guam and Manila lie far beyond it. Gillingham (ch. 6) gives up to five months for the outward voyage and about four for the return; Schurz and most accounts give about three months outward and four to six back.

sources.citation: William Lytle Schurz, The Manila Galleon (E. P. Dutton, 1939).
Arturo Giráldez, The Age of Trade: The Manila Galleons and the Dawn of the Global Economy (Rowman & Littlefield, 2015).
Paul Gillingham, Mexico: A 500-Year History (Atlantic Monthly Press, 2025), ch. 6.

properties.title: Manila galleon: the tornaviaje (return route)
properties.label: Tornaviaje
properties.description: The return was the hard part: the trade winds blow from the east, so ships leaving Manila in midsummer sailed northeast past Japan with the Kuroshio current to the westerlies of the North Pacific, crossed at around 35–40°N, and made landfall on the coast of California before running south past Baja California to Acapulco. The voyage took four to six months and scurvy killed many crews. The route is credited to Andrés de Urdaneta aboard the San Pedro, which reached Acapulco on 8 October 1565, but the small San Lucas, which had separated from Legazpi's fleet and was piloted by the free mulatto Lope Martín, had already made the crossing to Mexico some weeks earlier.
properties.note: Schematic: only the general track is drawn. The line begins at 130°W, the western edge of the map; the open-ocean path beyond it is not shown. Later galleons usually made landfall between about Cape Mendocino and Point Conception, moving south over time, and in the eighteenth century often stopped near Cabo San Lucas. Urdaneta's own landfall in 1565 was farther south, near the Channel Islands.

sources.citation: William Lytle Schurz, The Manila Galleon (E. P. Dutton, 1939).
Arturo Giráldez, The Age of Trade: The Manila Galleons and the Dawn of the Global Economy (Rowman & Littlefield, 2015).
Andrés Reséndez, Conquering the Pacific: An Unknown Mariner and the Final Great Voyage of the Age of Discovery (Houghton Mifflin Harcourt, 2021).
Paul Gillingham, Mexico: A 500-Year History (Atlantic Monthly Press, 2025), chs. 6 and 7.

properties.title: Veracruz moved to its present site
properties.label: Nueva Veracruz
properties.description: On royal orders and under the Conde de Monterrey, the town was moved from La Antigua to the beach of Chalchiuhcuecan opposite San Juan de Ulúa, where ships were actually loaded, roughly where Cortés had first landed in 1519. It received the title of city in the early seventeenth century and remained New Spain's only significant Atlantic port.
properties.note: Sources date the move to 1599 or 1600.

sources.citation: Peter Gerhard, A Guide to the Historical Geography of New Spain, rev. ed. (University of Oklahoma Press, 1993).
Paul Gillingham, Mexico: A 500-Year History (Atlantic Monthly Press, 2025), ch. 6.
